newsitem.title: CROATIA: Property issue may force Croatian Serb exodus.
newsitem.headline: Property issue may force Croatian Serb exodus.

text.p: Croatia's failure to establish a legal process allowing minority Serbs who fled war in 1995 to return home may spur a mass exodus from a last Serb enclave soon to be dissolved, a leading international human rights group says.

Almost 150,000 Serbs in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia voted on Sunday and Monday in regional elections supervised by a transitional U.N. administration created after Croatian troops reconquered rebel territory in western Croatia.
Croatian state institutions will be reinstated in Eastern Slavonia in the run-up to the July expiry of the U.N. mandate.

But Human Rights Watch-Helsinki said many Serbs may flee to nearby Serbia by then for fear of persecution, despite official guarantees of minority rights, and lack of alternative housing when Croat refugees from a 1991 war reclaim their homes.

Human Rights Watch noted that at least 60,000 of the almost 200,000 Krajina Serbs who fled the Croatian army blitz in 1995 holed up in Eastern Slavonia where they moved into empty housing which will now be reclaimed by Croat owners.

"The Croatian government has issued numerous, widely publicised statements and pledges, enthusiastically welcomed by the international community, guaranteeing the rights of ethnic Serbs in Eastern Slavonia.
"Yet it has failed to take steps necessary to permit the exercise of some of the most fundamental of these rights."

"If another mass exodus is to be avoided and widespread human rights abuses prevented, the Croatian government must undertake concrete measures that will give meaning to otherwise empty declarations of the right of displaced Serbs to return to original homes or remain in Eastern Slavonia."

Instead, Croatian authorities were busy resettling Croat refugees and migrants from Bosnia and Serbia in homes abandoned by Krajina Serbs. Croatian law did not set a time limit for how long such property can be occupied by a non-owner.

Human Rights Watch said a government plan for a two-way return of Croat and Serb refugees, drafted to placate Western critics, was "doomed to fail" if Zagreb pursued demographic engineering solidifying a new ethnically "pure" order.
Tensions had been further aggravated by the nationalist Croatian government's publication of lists of suspected Serb war criminals "which serve to intimidate the population", the report added.

U.N. administrators called for such lists to reassure Serbs that they would not be subject to a broad and arbitrary witchhunt avenging the seizure of Eastern Slavonia in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia.

But Human Rights Watch said UNTAES had not helped matters by engaging in negotiations over the size of the 'official' government list of suspects, saying such negotiations should be subject solely to legal considerations.

Human Rights Watch urged the United States and European Union to condition aid for Croatia's postwar reconstruction and membership in NATO's Partnership for Peace on a genuine effort by Zagreb to resettle minority citizens in safety and security.
